FROM BOGOTÁ TO JERUSALEM: COLOMBIA’S SHARP FOREIGN POLICY SHIFT

DOSYATM–ODAP/003

Colombia officially opened its embassy in Jerusalem on October 14, 2026, as part of its policy to reestablish relations with Israel. The ceremony was attended by Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar and Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar. Colombia became the tenth country to open an embassy in Jerusalem with this move. The Bogota government announced that they are rebuilding their previously severed relations with Israel and that they will continue their strategic partnership with Israel in this context. This step was condemned by 18 countries, including Turkey.

Colombia and Israel had been cooperating in many areas, especially security, for a long time. However, former President Gustavo Petro announced in May 2024 that they had severed diplomatic relations with Israel due to the Gaza war. Gustavo Petro had likened Israel's operations in the Gaza Strip to Nazi concentration camps and accused Israel of committing genocide. In this context, he had plans to open an embassy in Ramallah, West Bank. However, even though he could not implement this plan, he continued to stand against Israel's policies. However, President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office in August 2026 with the support of United States President Donald Trump, tried to repair the relations severed due to the Gaza war by opening an embassy in Jerusalem. With this move, he consciously reversed the previous administration's foreign policy actions.

The issue of Jerusalem has long been an unresolved matter between Palestine and Israel. Occupied Palestinians recognize East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war, as the capital of their future state, while Israel sees the entire city as its capital. There are also differing views in international politics regarding the status of Jerusalem. While many states keep their embassies in Tel Aviv, ten countries, including the United States, have moved their embassies to Jerusalem. In addition to all this, the United Nations Security Council's resolutions 476 and 478 from 1980 have deemed unilateral actions aimed at changing the city's status as invalid and have called for the withdrawal of diplomatic representatives from the city. In the context of these decisions, eighteen countries, led by Turkey, condemned Colombia, arguing that its decision undermined efforts for a two-state solution.

The long-term impact of the decision will depend on whether the reestablished partnership with Israel provides Colombia with tangible security, technology, and trade gains. Achieving visible results in these areas could facilitate the defense of the foreign policy change in domestic politics and its transformation into a more permanent state policy. Conversely, if the Jerusalem decision remains primarily a leader-centric and ideological choice, the diplomatic costs that may arise with Arab and Islamic countries could increase the likelihood of a subsequent administration changing the policy again.
